mcqs.q: Which feature of the 2017/2018 classification of periodontal and peri-implant diseases was NOT part of the earlier classifications?
opts: Periodontal health is itself included as a category
Gingival enlargement is recognised as a clinical finding
Plaque is accepted as the principal aetiological agent
mcqs.explain: The 2018 system is the first to classify health itself, on both an intact and a reduced periodontium.

mcqs.q: The primary parameter used to diagnose gingivitis in the 2018 classification is:
mcqs.explain: BOP is the primary diagnostic parameter; depth is used to confirm that the bleeding site is shallow.

mcqs.q: Which statement about reversibility is correct?
opts: Gingivitis reverts to health, but a periodontitis patient remains one for life
Both gingivitis and periodontitis revert to health once they have been treated
Neither reverts to health once attachment loss has already begun at a site
Periodontitis reverts to health once every probing depth falls below 4 mm
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis is reversible; a treated periodontitis patient is reclassified as a stable periodontitis patient, not as a healthy one.

mcqs.q: A new entity recognised by the 2018 classification is gingival inflammation:
opts: In a reduced periodontium after completion of periodontitis treatment
Confined to the interdental papilla only
Occurring in the complete absence of a dental biofilm
mcqs.explain: Inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a treated patient is now explicitly classified.

mcqs.q: Clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium is subdivided into a stable periodontitis patient and:
mcqs.explain: Recession and crown lengthening also reduce the periodontium without any history of periodontitis.

mcqs.q: Why must gingival health on a reduced periodontium in a stable periodontitis patient be distinguished from the same picture in a non-periodontitis patient?
opts: They differ in the risk for periodontal disease progression
Only one of them shows attachment loss on probing
Only one of them can present with bleeding on probing
mcqs.explain: The clinical picture can look identical; the risk of future progression is what separates them.

mcqs.q: In the case definition of periodontal health, the probing depth criterion on an INTACT periodontium is:
opts: No probing depth criterion is applied
mcqs.explain: An intact periodontium should have no site deeper than 3 mm.

mcqs.q: Health on a REDUCED periodontium permits a probing depth of:
opts: ≤ 4 mm, provided no 4 mm site bleeds on probing
≤ 4 mm, regardless of whether those sites bleed
≤ 3 mm, exactly as on an intact periodontium
≤ 5 mm, provided bone loss is not progressing
mcqs.explain: The 4 mm tolerance applies only to a non-bleeding site; a bleeding 4 mm site moves the patient out of health.

mcqs.q: The bleeding-on-probing score compatible with periodontal health is:
opts: Any score, provided no site exceeds 3 mm
mcqs.explain: A BOP score below 10% is the threshold for health in all three health columns.

mcqs.q: Radiographic bone loss in a patient with gingival health on a reduced periodontium but NO history of periodontitis is recorded as:
mcqs.explain: Recession or crown lengthening may or may not be accompanied by bone loss, so the table records it as possible.

mcqs.q: Probing attachment loss in the case definition of health on an intact periodontium is:
opts: Present at fewer than 10% of sites
mcqs.explain: By definition an intact periodontium shows no probing attachment loss.

mcqs.q: Gingival diseases and conditions are divided into which two broad categories?
opts: Dental plaque biofilm-induced and non–dental plaque-induced
mcqs.explain: The first split is by whether the dental biofilm is the cause.

mcqs.q: Localised plaque-induced gingivitis is defined by a bleeding-on-probing score of:
mcqs.explain: Below 10% is health; 10–30% is localised; above 30% is generalised.

mcqs.q: Generalised plaque-induced gingivitis is defined by a bleeding-on-probing score of:
mcqs.explain: The generalised threshold is above 30% of bleeding sites.

mcqs.q: The clinical signs of plaque-induced gingivitis are:
opts: Limited to the attached gingiva only
mcqs.explain: Erythema, oedema, bleeding, tenderness and enlargement are all gingival; the lesion does not extend beyond the gingiva.

mcqs.q: Which statement about attachment and bone loss in plaque-induced gingivitis is correct?
opts: The patient may or may not have experienced loss of attachment or bone
Loss of attachment must be absent for the diagnosis to be made
Bone loss must be present for the diagnosis to be made
Attachment loss must be present but bone loss must be absent
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis can occur on an intact or on a reduced periodontium, so previous loss is permitted.

mcqs.q: Plaque-induced gingivitis is reversed by:
mcqs.explain: There is a direct cause-and-effect relationship with the biofilm, so removing it resolves the lesion.

mcqs.q: Which of the following reduces the periodontium WITHOUT any history of periodontitis?
mcqs.explain: Crown lengthening and gingival recession both reduce the periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient.

mcqs.q: A successfully treated periodontitis patient who develops gingivitis has:
opts: An increased risk of periodontitis progression if the disease is not well controlled
The same risk of progression as a patient who never had periodontitis
No risk of progression once pockets have been eliminated
A risk that depends only on the number of remaining teeth
mcqs.explain: This is precisely why the treated patient is kept in a separate diagnostic category.

mcqs.q: The extent, severity and duration of the gingival inflammatory response can be altered by:
opts: Neither, as the response is determined solely by plaque mass
mcqs.explain: Both categories of modifying factor change how the host responds to the same biofilm challenge.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four subgroups of dental biofilm-induced gingivitis?
opts: Gingival disease mediated by systemic factors
mcqs.explain: The four subgroups are biofilm only, systemic factors, local factors and drug-induced enlargement.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis associated with the biofilm only is characterised by:
opts: A clear cause-and-effect relationship and full reversibility
A delayed response that persists after plaque removal
An exaggerated response out of proportion to the plaque present
An absence of bleeding on probing
mcqs.explain: This is the pure form: the biofilm alone explains the inflammation, and removing it resolves it.

mcqs.q: Systemic risk factors exacerbate the gingival inflammatory response through their effect on:
opts: The host's cellular and immunologic functions
The composition of the salivary pellicle
The thickness of the junctional epithelium only
The mineral content of the dental calculus
mcqs.explain: They act on the host, not on the quantity of biofilm.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a SYSTEMIC modifying factor for biofilm-induced gingival disease?
mcqs.explain: Hyperglycemia acts on the host response; the other three are local biofilm-retention factors.

mcqs.q: Sex steroid hormones modify the gingival response in all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: The listed sex-hormone states are puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy and oral contraceptives; oral dryness is listed separately as a local factor.

mcqs.q: Which group of systemic factors includes conditions such as leukaemia and anaemia?
mcqs.explain: Hematological conditions are one of the five listed systemic modifying factors.

mcqs.q: Local risk factors for gingival disease are best described as:
opts: Predisposing factors that allow biofilm to accumulate and be retained
Factors that amplify the immune response to a given biofilm
Factors that determine the virulence of the subgingival species
Factors that reduce the rate of calculus mineralisation
mcqs.explain: Local factors are predisposing — they put more biofilm in place; systemic factors modify the host response.

mcqs.q: The two local factors listed as mediating biofilm-induced gingival disease are:
opts: Biofilm retention factors and oral dryness
mcqs.explain: Biofilm retention factors (overhangs, crowding, calculus) and oral dryness are the two local headings.

mcqs.q: Which drug group causes gingival enlargement and is represented by phenytoin?
mcqs.explain: Phenytoin is the classical anticonvulsant associated with gingival enlargement.

mcqs.q: Cyclosporine-induced gingival enlargement falls under which drug group?
mcqs.explain: Cyclosporine is the example given for the immunosuppressive group.

mcqs.q: Nifedipine, verapamil and diltiazem all belong to which group of enlargement-inducing drugs?
mcqs.explain: All three are calcium channel blockers, the third drug group in the classification.

mcqs.q: Drug-influenced gingival enlargement is best described as:
opts: Patient specific and influenced by uncontrolled plaque accumulation
An inevitable consequence of the drug, independent of oral hygiene
Dependent only on the dose and duration of the drug
Restricted to patients with pre-existing periodontitis
mcqs.explain: Not every patient on the drug is affected, and poor plaque control makes it worse — so hygiene is a target of management.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis is defined as bleeding at a site of ≤ 3 mm rather than ≤ 4 mm because:
opts: A treated patient with bleeding sites stays at high risk of recurrence
A site measuring 4 mm cannot be probed reproducibly from visit to visit
A site measuring 4 mm never bleeds while attachment loss is still absent
Any depth greater than 3 mm is by definition a diagnosis of periodontitis
mcqs.explain: The stricter shallow-site criterion protects against calling a high-risk bleeding treated patient merely gingivitic.

mcqs.q: In the case definition of gingivitis, the probing depth criterion in ALL three columns is:
opts: It varies with the state of the periodontium
mcqs.explain: Unlike the health table, the gingivitis table applies the ≤ 3 mm criterion uniformly.

mcqs.q: Which parameter differs between the case definitions of health and of gingivitis on a reduced periodontium?
opts: The probing depth and the BOP score
The presence of probing attachment loss
The presence of radiographic bone loss
None — only the clinical appearance differs
mcqs.explain: Attachment loss and bone loss are present in both; the depth criterion and the bleeding score distinguish them.

mcqs.q: How many groups of non–dental biofilm-induced gingival diseases does the 2018 classification list?
mcqs.explain: Genetic/developmental, specific infections, inflammatory and immune, reactive, neoplasms, endocrine/nutritional/metabolic, traumatic and pigmentation.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a group of non–dental biofilm-induced gingival diseases?
mcqs.explain: Reactive processes are one of the eight non-biofilm groups; the others listed are biofilm-induced subgroups.

mcqs.q: Gingival pigmentation is classified as:
opts: A local modifying factor of plaque-induced gingivitis
mcqs.explain: It is the eighth group of non-biofilm-induced gingival diseases and conditions.

mcqs.q: The mode of inheritance of hereditary gingival fibromatosis is:
opts: Autosomal dominant, or rarely autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive, or rarely autosomal dominant
mcqs.explain: Autosomal dominant transmission predominates, with rare autosomal recessive forms.

mcqs.q: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis may:
opts: Completely cover the teeth and delay eruption
Resolve spontaneously after puberty in every case
Occur only as part of a generalized syndrome
mcqs.explain: The overgrowth may bury the crowns and delay eruption, and may be isolated or syndrome-associated.

mcqs.q: Which organisms cause the bacterial specific infections of the gingiva named in the classification?
mcqs.explain: Gonorrhoea and syphilis organisms are the named bacterial causes, along with streptococcal gingivitis or gingivostomatitis.

mcqs.q: Oral candidiasis as a non-biofilm gingival disease is particularly seen in:
opts: The immunocompromised, and users of long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics
Patients carrying heavy supragingival calculus on the lower anterior teeth
Patients taking a calcium channel blocker for more than three months
Patients with the autosomal-dominant form of hereditary gingival fibromatosis
mcqs.explain: Reduced immunity and a disturbed commensal flora are the two predisposing circumstances listed.

mcqs.q: Streptococcal gingivitis or gingivostomatitis is classified as:
opts: A specific infection of bacterial origin
A biofilm-induced gingivitis mediated by local factors
mcqs.explain: It is listed with the bacterial specific infections, not with plaque-induced disease.

mcqs.q: Inflammatory and immune gingival conditions typically present as:
opts: Desquamative lesions, ulcerations of the gingiva, or both
Firm fibrous enlargement covering the crowns
Localised blue-black pigmentation of the marginal gingiva
Pedunculated exophytic masses at the papilla
mcqs.explain: Desquamation and ulceration are the characteristic presentations; allergic reactions are included in this group.

mcqs.q: Allergic reactions of the gingiva are classified under:
mcqs.explain: They sit with the inflammatory and immune conditions in the non-biofilm group.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the three listed types of traumatic gingival lesion?
mcqs.explain: The three listed are factitious/self-inflicted, iatrogenic and accidental.

mcqs.q: A localised gingival dehiscence produced by a patient habitually picking the tissue with a fingernail is classified as:
opts: Plaque-induced gingivitis mediated by a local factor
mcqs.explain: Damage produced deliberately or habitually by the patient is factitious and self-inflicted.

mcqs.q: Damage to the gingiva caused during a dental procedure is classified as:
mcqs.explain: Iatrogenic means produced by the treatment or the operator.

mcqs.q: Which reference is the source for this classification lecture?
opts: Newman and Carranza's Clinical Periodontology and Implantology, 14th edition, Chapter 5
Lindhe's Clinical Periodontology and Implant Dentistry, 7th edition
Wilson and Kornman's Fundamentals of Periodontics
mcqs.explain: Chapter 5 of Newman and Carranza, 14th edition, from page 61.

saqs.q: List the four features that the 2017/2018 classification of periodontal and peri-implant diseases introduced.
saqs.a: Periodontal health is included in the classification; bleeding on probing is the primary parameter for diagnosing gingivitis; gingival inflammation in a reduced periodontium after completed periodontitis treatment is recognised; and gingivitis can revert to health whereas a periodontitis patient remains a periodontitis patient for life.

list: Periodontal health is included — health itself is now a category.
Bleeding on probing is the primary parameter to diagnose gingivitis.
Gingival inflammation in a reduced periodontium — after completion of treatment of a periodontitis patient.
Gingivitis reverts to health; periodontitis does not — a periodontitis patient remains one for life.

saqs.q: Outline the subdivisions of periodontal and gingival health in the 2018 classification.
saqs.a: Clinical gingival health on an intact periodontium; and clinical gingival health on a reduced periodontium, subdivided into the stable periodontitis patient and the non-periodontitis patient.

list: a. On an intact periodontium — clinical gingival health.
b. On a reduced periodontium — clinical gingival health, subdivided into: i. stable periodontitis patient; ii. non-periodontitis patient (e.g. recession, crown lengthening).

ans.text: The distinction matters because the two differ in their risk for periodontal disease progression.

saqs.q: Give the case definition of periodontal health for an intact and for a reduced periodontium.
saqs.a: Intact: no attachment loss, no radiographic bone loss, probing depth ≤3 mm at all sites, BOP <10%. Reduced with a history of periodontitis: attachment loss and bone loss present, probing depth ≤4 mm with no 4 mm site bleeding, BOP <10%. Reduced without a history of periodontitis: attachment loss present, bone loss possible, probing depth ≤3 mm, BOP <10%.

head: Intact
Reduced
Reduced, no periodontitis history
rows: ≤ 4 mm — no 4 mm site with BOP

saqs.q: Compare the case definitions of health and of gingivitis on a reduced periodontium.
saqs.a: Both show probing attachment loss and radiographic bone loss. Health allows ≤4 mm provided no 4 mm site bleeds and requires BOP <10%; gingivitis requires ≤3 mm with BOP 10–30% if localised or >30% if generalised.

ans.text: Gingivitis is defined at ≤ 3 mm because a treated periodontitis patient who develops bleeding sites remains at high risk of recurrence and progressive attachment loss.

saqs.q: Describe the clinical characteristics of plaque biofilm-induced gingivitis.
saqs.a: It is confined to the gingiva, with erythema, oedema, bleeding, tenderness and enlargement; it is reversed when plaque is removed; it is associated with high bacterial plaque and with systemic modifying factors; and the patient may or may not have experienced loss of attachment or bone.

list: Confined to the gingiva — erythema, oedema, bleeding, tenderness, enlargement.
Associated with high bacterial plaque and with systemic modifying factors.
The patient may or may not have experienced loss of attachment or bone.

saqs.q: State the bleeding-on-probing thresholds that separate health, localised gingivitis and generalised gingivitis.
saqs.a: Health is below 10% of bleeding sites, localised gingivitis is 10–30%, and generalised gingivitis is more than 30%.

saqs.q: How is gingivitis classified at the site level?
saqs.a: Gingivitis on an intact periodontium; and gingivitis on a reduced periodontium, either in a non-periodontitis patient (recession, crown lengthening) or in a successfully treated periodontitis patient, who carries an increased risk of progression if the disease is not well controlled.

list: 2. On a reduced periodontium — a. non-periodontitis patient (recession, crown lengthening); b. successfully treated periodontitis patient, with an increased risk of periodontitis progression if the disease is not well controlled.

saqs.q: List the four subgroups of dental biofilm-induced gingivitis.
saqs.a: Gingivitis associated with biofilm only; gingival diseases mediated by systemic factors; gingival diseases mediated by local factors; and drug-induced gingival enlargement.

list: Gingivitis associated with biofilm only — a clear cause-and-effect relationship, fully reversible.

saqs.q: Distinguish systemic from local modifying factors of biofilm-induced gingival disease, and give the examples of each.
saqs.a: Systemic risk factors exacerbate the inflammatory response through effects on the host's cellular and immunologic functions: smoking, hyperglycemia, nutritional factors, hematological conditions and sex steroid hormones (puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, oral contraceptives). Local risk factors are predisposing: biofilm retention factors such as overhanging restorations, crowding and calculus, and oral dryness.

head: Systemic (modifying)
Local (predisposing)
rows: exacerbate the response via the host's cellular and immunologic functions
allow biofilm to accumulate and be retained
smoking · hyperglycemia · nutritional factors · hematological conditions · sex steroid hormones (puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, oral contraceptives)
biofilm retention factors — overhanging restorations, crowding, calculus · oral dryness

saqs.q: Name the three drug groups that cause gingival enlargement, give one example of each, and state two qualifying features of the condition.
saqs.a: Anticonvulsants (phenytoin), immunosuppressives (cyclosporine) and calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, verapamil, diltiazem). It is patient specific and is influenced by uncontrolled plaque accumulation.

list: It is influenced by uncontrolled plaque accumulation.

saqs.q: List the eight groups of non–dental biofilm-induced gingival diseases.
saqs.a: Genetic/developmental disorders; specific infections; inflammatory and immune conditions; reactive processes; neoplasms; endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases; traumatic lesions; and gingival pigmentation.

A genetic/developmental disorder of the periodontal tissues inherited in an autosomal-dominant or, rarely, autosomal-recessive manner. The gingival enlargement may completely cover the teeth and delay eruption, and may present as an isolated finding or be associated with generalized syndromes.

list: Inheritance — autosomal dominant, or rarely autosomal recessive.
Presentation — enlargement that may completely cover the teeth and delay eruption.
Associations — may be an isolated finding or associated with generalized syndromes.

saqs.q: Classify the specific infections of the gingiva with their examples.
saqs.a: Bacterial — Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Treponema pallidum, and streptococcal gingivitis or gingivostomatitis. Viral — gingival diseases of viral origin. Fungal — candidiasis, in immunocompromised individuals and in those whose microbiota is disturbed by long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics.

head: Origin
Examples
rows: candidiasis — in immunocompromised individuals and with a microbiota disturbed by long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics

saqs.q: How do inflammatory and immune gingival conditions present, and what are the three types of traumatic gingival lesion?
saqs.a: Inflammatory and immune conditions present as desquamative lesions, ulcerations of the gingiva, or both, and allergic reactions are included in this group. The traumatic lesions are self-inflicted and factitious, iatrogenic trauma, and self-inflicted accidental damage.

list: Present as desquamative lesions, ulcerations of the gingiva, or both.
